source: Pontis & Blandford (2016) Understanding influence: an empirical test of the data-frame theory of sensemaking (JASIST)
finding: Test of the data-frame (D/F) model on a new task type. Think-aloud study of academics making sense of who is influential, in a familiar field (HCI) and an unfamiliar one (chemistry).
numbers: 11 participants: 6 novice MSc students (1-5 y experience), 5 experts (more than 10 y). 4 tasks each = 44 tasks (2 identify, 2 predict). Sessions 50-90 min. 16 tasks from 4 people (N4, N6, E2, E3) coded in depth; stopped when task 13 onward added nothing new. Two coders, consensus.
limits: Qualitative. Four people analysed in depth, one task type (name 3 people), one discipline. It is coding of transcripts to the model, not a prediction that could fail.
agent_relevance: Shows how the theory has been tested so far: by fitting coded transcripts to the box diagram. Do not count this as strong evidence for causal claims.

source: Pontis & Blandford (2016) Understanding influence: an empirical test of the data-frame theory of sensemaking (JASIST)
finding: In all 44 tasks people worked with only ONE frame. No participant reframed. They grew the same structure by adding indicators (anchors). Three D/F activities never appeared: seeking and inferring new relationships, tracking anomalies, seeking a new frame.
numbers: 44 tasks; 0 reframings; 3 of the model's activities unobserved; 11 activities coded = 9 from Klein et al. 2007 plus 2 new (preselecting candidates, making the final choice).
limits: Klein et al. (2007) say sensemakers compare up to 3 frames in narrative tasks; this task had no story to rebuild, so no rival explanation arose.
agent_relevance: Reframing is not universal. It needs data that contradict the frame. Supports G1: reframe only on a signal. A frame that keeps filling in with no conflict should just be elaborated.

source: Pontis & Blandford (2016) Understanding influence: an empirical test of the data-frame theory of sensemaking (JASIST)
finding: Lists the D/F cognitive activities as given in Klein et al. (2007, pp. 132-142): mapping data and frame; elaborating a frame; questioning a frame; preserving a frame; comparing frames; reframing; constructing or finding a frame. They can start in any order; a sensemaker may use a few or all.
numbers: 7 activities here (the 'six frame activities' in other summaries drop mapping). Max 3 alternative frames compared at once per Klein 2007; this paper says Klein gives no explanation for the limit of three.
quote: A frame should not be preserved if indicators of inaccuracy emerge during the exploration process.
limits: Secondhand description of the 2007 chapter; the chapter itself was not opened.
agent_relevance: A clean activity list. Map each to a program-checked move on one stored frame: elaborate = fill a slot; question = a check failed; preserve = log the anomaly as not relevant; compare = score two frames; reframe = replace; seek = generate a new frame.

source: Pontis & Blandford (2016) Understanding influence: an empirical test of the data-frame theory of sensemaking (JASIST)
finding: Experts versus novices on the same tasks. Experts made longer journeys with more turning points, questioned source quality, discarded more data points, and elaborated the frame before accepting a name. Novices picked names fast, with fewer questioning steps, and compared several candidates at the end.
numbers: Task 3 example: N6 used 6 data points and preselected 6 names; E2 used 15 data points. Participants preselected 3 to 8 candidates per task; most picked exactly the requested 3.
limits: Two people illustrate each group. In their own field experts relied on prior knowledge (soft evidence) while novices sought hard evidence.
agent_relevance: Matches Klein's claim that experts differ in repertoire, not process. Questioning data quality before accepting a candidate is a cheap move to copy: re-check a source or recompute before keeping a hypothesis.

source: Pontis & Blandford (2016) Understanding influence: an empirical test of the data-frame theory of sensemaking (JASIST)
finding: Authors propose a revised D/F figure for structure tasks: activities act on frame instantiations (candidate names), and cycles grow from 3 to 5 (adds an analysis cycle and a decision-making cycle). They add explicit start (recognise the situation, build an initial frame) and end boxes, which the original lacks.
numbers: 3 cycles to 5 cycles; 2 added activities. They cite Moore & Hoffman (2011) that the model has 'no box that says start here'.
limits: Proposal only, not tested on new data.
agent_relevance: The original diagram has no start, stop or order. An implementation must supply its own. Our schema does: entry S1, exit S8 by code check, order chosen by the program.

source: Rankin, Woltjer & Field (2016) Sensemaking following surprise in the cockpit: a re-framing problem (Cogn Tech Work 18:623)
finding: Interview study of how airline pilots handle surprises, coded with D/F activities.
numbers: 20 pilots (14 were instructors or examiners; mean 10,892 flight hours; mean age 49). Semi-structured critical-incident interviews of 50-90 min. 48 surprise cases extracted; 9 analysed in detail; 9 challenge categories.
limits: Retrospective self-report, mostly senior Western European pilots; no counts of activities across the 48 cases. Authors note memory distortion and self-protection risks.
agent_relevance: Shows D/F applied to real high-stakes cases; frame activities are visible in how people recount surprises.

source: Rankin, Woltjer & Field (2016) Sensemaking following surprise in the cockpit: a re-framing problem (Cogn Tech Work 18:623)
finding: Pilots used questioning, preserving, elaborating and comparing frames, in messy sequences (question, seek, preserve, re-question, elaborate, compare within a short time). Elaborating and comparing sometimes ran at the same time. The authors add two activities missing from the 2007 model: rapid frame-switching and abandoning the search for a frame.
numbers: 2 new activities beyond the 2007 list. Rapid switching shown in cases 2, 5, 7; abandoning the search shown in cases 1, 3, 7, 8 (their table).
limits: Case-based; no frequencies.
agent_relevance: Activities are not clean separate steps. Allow several to be open at once (one frame being elaborated while a rival is scored). Add two outcomes to impasse handling: drop the explain goal and fall back to a known procedure; switch at once to a stored alternative frame when time is short.

source: Rankin, Woltjer & Field (2016) Sensemaking following surprise in the cockpit: a re-framing problem (Cogn Tech Work 18:623)
finding: Case 3 shows the whole loop. The crew treated the first warning as a system fault (preserve), more faults came (question), they tried to explain them (elaborate), found no plausible frame, then took manual control with a known frame. This is abandoning the search for a frame.
numbers: Pilot sayings: 'identify what you have, not what you don't have'; 'sit on your hands' and evaluate.
limits: Interview accounts; one case. Authors say knowing when to stop troubleshooting is hard.
agent_relevance: Maps to schema S6 impasse and G6 (never abstain): when explanation fails, switch the goal to controlling the outcome with a known procedure and submit the best attempt.

source: Rankin, Woltjer & Field (2016) Sensemaking following surprise in the cockpit: a re-framing problem (Cogn Tech Work 18:623)
finding: The frame decides what is noticed. A cue that is not salient or not expected is missed, and slow ('passive and insidious') changes give no surprise, so nothing triggers questioning. Surprise is the trigger when it does occur.
numbers: 9 challenge categories, incl. absence of salient cues, passive disturbances, conflicting data, getting stuck in a narrow frame, sudden changes, insufficient system knowledge. Case 1: crew forgot the second autopilot and after go-around believed the autopilot was flying.
limits: Single interview-based categorisation. The paper repeats the known tendency to rationalise anomalies (fixation error; De Keyser & Woods 1990; Sarter et al. 1997), which I did not open.
agent_relevance: The main risk for an LLM is no trigger: no check fails, so G1 never fires. Add checks that sample data the frame does not predict (G3).

source: Rankin, Woltjer & Field (2016) Sensemaking following surprise in the cockpit: a re-framing problem (Cogn Tech Work 18:623)
finding: Claims about experts: an expert is not someone who interprets data better but someone who recognises the right cues to break a frame and find a new one. Restates Klein et al. (2007): experts and novices share the reasoning process and differ in the knowledge base.
numbers: Cites Feltovich et al. 1997 and Malakis & Kontogiannis 2013 (air traffic controllers: experts better than novices at applying criteria that spot subtle cues). Neither opened.
limits: Cited findings, secondhand.
agent_relevance: Supports a stored library of frames with cue-to-frame tests, rather than a better 'reasoning style'.

source: Zheng, Miller, Bialkowski, Soyer & Janda (2025) Supporting data-frame dynamics in AI-assisted decision making (arXiv 2504.15894)
finding: A small formal model of D/F for AI decision support. Raw information gives evidence e_t by an extraction function; a retrieval function gives a hypothesis set H_t; a score s(e,h) in [0,1] rates each hypothesis. If the best score is below a threshold tau, either extract more evidence or retrieve more hypotheses, and repeat until some score reaches tau.
numbers: Formulas only. Prototype: concept bottleneck model on derm7pt skin-lesion data (7 dermoscopy concepts), conformal prediction for the hypothesis set. No user study yet (planned with dermatologists).
limits: Workshop paper, 6 pages, no results. Covers fit, elaborate and seek only; no explicit preserve, compare or reframe operator. A frame is a hypothesis from a candidate set.
agent_relevance: The only explicit loop I found close to code. A skeleton for S2 to S4: extract, retrieve candidate rules, score on held-out data, loop on a threshold. Threshold and scoring must come from code checks, not the model's opinion (G5).

source: Zheng, Miller, Bialkowski, Soyer & Janda (2025) Supporting data-frame dynamics in AI-assisted decision making (arXiv 2504.15894)
finding: Mixed-initiative design from D/F: human and AI can each intervene on three functions (evidence extraction, hypothesis retrieval, hypothesis scoring). Users edit evidence and the system updates hypotheses, instead of accepting or rejecting one recommendation.
numbers: Interface with 3 views (image, evidence, diagnosis). Claimed benefits (less over-reliance, lower load) are stated as aims, not measured.
limits: No evaluation. Builds on Miller (2023) evaluative AI.
agent_relevance: Idea for the multiplayer plan: people edit evidence or add a candidate frame, the agent re-scores. Untested; test before trusting.

source: Lebiere, Pirolli, Thomson, Paik, Rutledge-Taylor, Staszewski & Anderson (2013) A functional model of sensemaking in a neurocognitive architecture
finding: The main computational model that cites D/F. An ACT-R model of the AHA geospatial intelligence tasks (six tasks) reproduces four biases: confirmation, anchoring and adjustment, representativeness, probability matching. The biases are not coded in; they arise from blended memory retrieval, the task and strategies.
numbers: Compared with 45 MITRE employees. Overall R2 = .645 for Negentropy across tasks. On a new dataset (Penn State students with geospatial coursework) Negentropy R2 = .591.
limits: Fit is mixed per task: S1 score R2 was .929 (task 1), .313 (task 2), .001 (task 3). The model does probability updating; it has no explicit reframing operator. The intro lists elaboration, questioning, reframing only as background.
agent_relevance: Confirmation is defined as a distribution peakier than the Bayes optimum and anchoring as flatter. A measurable pair we could apply to our own probability outputs.

source: Lebiere, Pirolli, Thomson, Paik, Rutledge-Taylor, Staszewski & Anderson (2013) A functional model of sensemaking in a neurocognitive architecture
finding: Mechanism for the biases: blended retrieval over past instances regresses to the mean, giving anchoring at high probabilities and confirmation at low ones; centroid-of-centroids anchors on early judgments; negative feedback on forced winner-take-all leads to probability matching later.
numbers: Table 3 lists 5 functions: centroid generation, path planning, probability adjustment, resource allocation, layer selection. One model with the same parameters on tasks 1-6.
limits: Synthetic map data, not open-ended explanation.
agent_relevance: Early experience fixes later bias. Do not feed a first answer into later attempts; keep attempts independent (G4).

source: Militello et al. (2018) Understanding how primary care clinicians make sense of chronic pain (Cogn Tech Work)
finding: D/F used as a coding scheme in medicine. Critical Decision Method interviews with primary care clinicians about chronic-pain patients. Found sets of anchors (patient behaviours, condition, goals, opioid history; social and environmental factors) and clinician factors that shape the frame.
numbers: 10 clinicians, 30 patients, interviews within 2 days of the visit; 61 segments from the first 15 transcripts card-sorted by a team.
limits: Descriptive; one health system; no outcome measure. Authors say earlier D/F work was mostly description. They picked D/F over heuristics-and-biases because no normative treatment could be defined.
agent_relevance: Anchors are a loggable data type: which 3-4 facts made the first frame. If those are wrong, the frame is wrong.

source: Klein, Jalaeian, Hoffman & Mueller (2023) The plausibility transition model for sensemaking (Front Psychol)
finding: Klein's own later model adds plausibility judgments to D/F. People test a causal story state by state; plausibility gaps (known causes do not explain the next state) cause strain and drive information search or dismissal of anomalous data. Closure is abrupt.
numbers: Built from 23 of 73 explanation cases, one reviewer (the senior author). Literature search: 1,042 articles, 18 strongly relevant plus 4 added.
quote: statistical analysis of outliers is a misleading and insufficient treatment of anomaly detection
limits: No statistics; convenience sample; exploratory and untested; the story form oversimplifies multi-cause cases. Content read through a page fetch summary.
agent_relevance: Suggests a computable proxy: count unexplained transitions in the current rule (gaps) and reframe when the count passes a threshold. Needs testing on our logs.

source: Klein, Jalaeian, Hoffman & Mueller (2023) The plausibility transition model for sensemaking (Front Psychol)
finding: Two stated predictions: closing a plausibility gap should be abrupt, not gradual; as anomalies are explained away, strain rises until people become skeptical and either search for an alternative or become receptive to one they had dismissed. Example: on the USS Vincennes, the airliner story was rejected because explaining away the data took too much effort.
numbers: No predictions were tested in the paper.
limits: Hypothesis-and-theory article. Competes with a fixed anomaly-count account: here change is driven by effort of explaining away.
agent_relevance: Two candidate triggers to test on our logs: anomaly count versus explain-away effort (steps or tokens spent justifying a failed check).

source: Prochaska et al. (2024) Misleading ourselves: how disinformation manipulates sensemaking (arXiv 2410.14858)
finding: Takes frame fixation from Klein et al. (2007) as being stuck on a single explanation. Applies D/F to online election rumours and argues frames come in clusters tied to a deep story, so a swapped frame (fraud to disenfranchisement) leaves the underlying story intact.
numbers: About 1,000 coded tweets: 100 per rumour, 5 rumours, 500 per year (2020 and 2022 elections).
limits: Qualitative human data. Not an LLM study and not a test of D/F.
agent_relevance: A reframe that keeps the same assumptions is no reframe. Require the new rule to differ from the old on a stated assumption and fit a held-out case (code check).

source: Matuschak reading notes on Klein, Phillips, Rall & Peluso (2007) A data-frame theory of sensemaking (secondary summary page)
finding: Secondary summary of Klein, Phillips, Rall & Peluso (2007). Frame: 'an explanatory structure that defines entities by describing their relationship to other entities'. Sensemaking: fitting data into a frame and fitting a frame around the data. Frame forms: story, map, script, plan; a mental model is a causal kind of frame. Data and frame are co-constructed; frames define what counts as data. Sensemaking ends when no key data are unexplained and no key frame element is ambiguous.
numbers: Initial frame built from about 3-4 anchor data elements (p. 123 per the note-taker). 8 functions of sensemaking listed (p. 117).
limits: A personal notes page, not the chapter. The chapter's field cases are not described.
agent_relevance: Gives a stopping rule we can code: all key data explained and no open slots in the frame. Matches S8 verify. Experts share the reasoning process; they hold a richer frame repertoire.

source: Wikipedia: Sensemaking (information science)
finding: Says Klein et al. (2006b) treat sensemaking as starting when an individual or organisation recognises its understanding is inadequate. Notes parallels to the recognition-metacognition model (Cohen et al. 1996) and Piaget (assimilation, accommodation), both tagged as unsourced.
numbers: No experiments or numbers on the page.
limits: Encyclopedia page; no frame activities and no empirical test listed.
agent_relevance: No easy open summary of empirical results exists; the evidence has to be pieced together from application studies.

source: Klein, Moon & Hoffman (2006) Making sense of sensemaking 2: a macrocognitive model, IEEE Intelligent Systems 21(5):88-92
finding: The short founding paper with the D/F diagram. NOT opened: no free copy found. The diagram is reproduced in Lebiere et al. 2013 and Militello et al. 2018, whose text I read.
numbers: OpenAlex metadata: about 570 citations.
limits: Everything about it here comes from papers that cite it.
agent_relevance: Get the diagram and the activity definitions from the paper itself before fixing schema wording.

source: Klein, Phillips, Rall & Peluso (2007) A data-frame theory of sensemaking, in Expertise Out of Context (NDM6), pp. 113-155
finding: The long founding chapter with the case analysis behind the theory. NOT opened: paywalled, no open copy found. Known only via Pontis & Blandford 2016, Rankin et al. 2016, the Matuschak notes and Prochaska et al. 2024.
numbers: OpenAlex metadata: about 326 citations. Details cited by others: 7 activities at pp. 132-142, up to 3 frames compared, 3-4 anchors, frame fixation, just-in-time frames.
limits: I could not check case counts or any incident-level result. No controlled experiment is described by any secondary source.
agent_relevance: Highest-value unread source. Needed to answer: in the field cases how often was a frame preserved versus replaced, and what predicted each.

source: Pirolli & Card (2005) The sensemaking process and leverage points for analyst technology identified through cognitive task analysis
finding: A cognitive task analysis of intelligence analysts giving two loops: an information foraging loop and a sensemaking loop (schema, hypotheses, presentation). Lebiere et al. 2013 says it used a conceptual model like D/F. From memory plus that citation; not opened.
numbers: None recalled with confidence.
limits: Memory only; unverified.
agent_relevance: Related but separate model; D/F's frame corresponds roughly to its schema. Foraging versus sensemaking maps to gather (S1, S3) versus represent and test (S2, S4).

source: Chinn & Brewer (1993) The role of anomalous data in knowledge acquisition (Review of Educational Research 63)
finding: A taxonomy of seven responses to anomalous data: ignore, reject, exclude from the theory's domain, hold in abeyance, reinterpret, make a peripheral change, change the theory. From memory; not opened. A finer account of what D/F calls preserve and reframe.
numbers: 7 responses.
limits: Memory only; verify before use. Based on students facing science anomalies, not field experts.
agent_relevance: Gives a finer menu for a failed check than one 'preserve'. Only 'change the theory' should reset the frame.

source: Pontis & Blandford (2016) Understanding influence: an empirical test of the data-frame theory of sensemaking (JASIST)
finding: Describes earlier D/F work: intelligence analysis (Moore & Hoffman 2011), Bosnia peacekeeping scenarios and navigation (Sieck et al. 2007), medical operative sensemaking (Stewart et al. 2011), problem detection (Klein et al. 2005), incident analysis. States that very few studies had examined structure tasks.
numbers: 5 earlier application areas. Moore & Hoffman's title (seen in Zheng et al. references): D/F 'as a best model for intelligence'.
limits: All these cited works were not opened by me. Earlier work was on narrative tasks.
agent_relevance: Evidence for D/F is breadth of application, not tests that could refute it. Treat it as a descriptive vocabulary and test our use of it on our own logs (G7).
